status.en: 13 armed incidents reported in the past seven days, 30% more than the week before, most of them in Caracas, Valencia and Maracaibo.

summary.en: Lawmakers have opened Venezuela's crisis-hit power sector to private investment, shifting from previous state control, while Brazil and Venezuela have agreed to upgrade ties through oil investment talks and Fluor has returned to the country after a two-decade hiatus. The United States managed $12 billion in Venezuelan oil revenue and secret talks involving a Trump aide have been linked to Vitol's win in crude sales rights. Delcy Rodríguez and Lula da Silva have pledged to fully reactivate bilateral ties, and Conviasa will resume flights to Cuba despite fuel shortages on the island. The conflict environment still records 2 battle-related deaths in 2007, according to UCDP.
summary.nb: Lovgivere har åpnet Venezuelas kriseplagede kraftsektor for privat investering, og går bort fra tidligere statlig kontroll, mens Brasil og Venezuela har blitt enige om å styrke båndene gjennom oljeinvesteringssamtaler og Fluor har vendt tilbake til landet etter et to tiår langt fravær. USA håndterte 12 milliarder dollar i venezuelansk oljeinntekt, og hemmelige samtaler med en Trump-assistent har blitt knyttet til Vitols seier i rettighetene til råoljesalg. Delcy Rodríguez og Lula da Silva har lovet å fullt ut gjenoppta bilaterale forbindelser, og Conviasa vil gjenoppta flyvninger til Cuba til tross for drivstoffmangel på øya. Konfliktsituasjonen registrerer fortsatt to dødsfall i kamper i 2007, ifølge UCDP.

background.title: Crisis in Venezuela
background.extract: An ongoing socioeconomic and political crisis began in Venezuela during the presidencies of Hugo Chávez, Nicolás Maduro as well as Delcy Rodríguez. It has been marked by hyperinflation, starvation, disease, crime, and mortality rates, resulting in massive emigration. Food shortages and hyperinflation have ended, but inflation remains high. It is the worst economic crisis in Venezuela's history and considered by some sources as more severe than the Great Depression in the United States, the 1985–1994 Brazilian economic crisis, or the 2008–2009 hyperinflation in Zimbabwe. In 2019, the Institute of International Finance called it the single largest economic collapse outside of war in 45 years. Writers have compared aspects, such as unemployment and GDP contraction, to Bosnia and Herzegovina after the 1992–95 Bosnian War, and those in Russia, Cuba and Albania following the Revolutions of 1989.
